idiom_name: chan T - language-level channel, each value to exactly one receive
implementation_notes: A Go channel is the point-to-point channel: the language matches every send to exactly one receive (the memory model states each send is synchronized before the completion of its corresponding receive), a buffered channel is the queue, and adding consumers is literally starting more goroutines that range over the same channel - no dispatcher library, no locks. Channel direction types (chan<-, <-chan) keep only one end visible to each side, so the contract is part of the signature. A broker-backed queue is needed only when messages must survive process failure or leave the host.
code_sketch:
jobs := make(chan Job, 64)                 // bounded channel = the queue
for i := 0; i < 4; i++ {                   // competing consumers
    go func() { for j := range jobs { handle(j) } }()
}
for _, j := range batch { jobs <- j }      // sender never picks a receiver
close(jobs)                                // sender side closes
pitfalls: Sending on a closed channel panics and only the sender side may close; a consumer that closes turns ordinary shutdown into intermittent crashes.
An unbuffered channel blocks the send until a receiver is ready - right for hand-off, wrong when the channel must absorb bursts.
A range consumer loop ends only when the channel is closed; forgetting it leaks goroutines silently until shutdown.
